abstract: A model based on two centuries of technological change predicts that artificial intelligence will produce fundamentally different labor market effects than past innovations. While historical technological advances benefited higher-education, higher-wage occupations with more female workers by substituting for physical labor, AI's substitution for cognitive tasks will shift demand toward lower-education, lower-wage occupations with a greater share of male workers. The overall productivity gains from AI will indirectly benefit workers in manual and interpersonal task occupations not directly affected by AI.
keyFindings: Past technological advances from 1850-2010 tended to benefit occupations with higher educational requirements, higher wages, and a greater fraction of female workers by substituting for physical labor.

AI will shift relative demand toward occupations with lower education, lower wages, and a greater share of male workers because it substitutes primarily for cognitive tasks rather than physical labor.
The overall economic growth and productivity generated by AI will indirectly benefit workers in jobs focused on manual or interpersonal tasks that are not negatively affected by AI substitution.

AI's impact on specific occupations depends on the extent to which it affects specific tasks—some occupations like bookkeeping may see most tasks substituted while others like medicine may see only partial task substitution, freeing workers for higher-value activities.
Age disparities in skill acquisition may emerge, with younger workers better able to acquire new skills needed for AI-enhanced occupations while older workers risk being left behind.
methodology: The authors analyzed patent documents from 1850 to 2010 to identify past technological improvements. They used a state-of-the-art large language model with web-search capabilities to track how innovations affected task descriptions for U.S. Census Bureau occupations over time. These historical insights were then applied to model how AI could affect employment trends over the next 10 to 20 years.
qualifiers: The paper presents model-based projections about potential future labor market effects over the next 10 to 20 years. The specific occupational impacts will depend on the extent to which AI affects particular tasks within occupations, which varies considerably. The analysis notes that outcomes for younger versus older workers may differ based on ability to acquire new skills.
